title: Why Your User Story Isn't Actually "Done"
description:
A user story sounds finished the moment the template is filled in -- but without acceptance criteria, "done" is just a guess. This Short breaks down the Given/When/Then format for acceptance criteria, straight from the Writing Requirements lesson in the Product Manager Mastery Path, and why skipping it is where scope arguments quietly start.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/product-manager-mastery-path/level-1/05-writing-requirements/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Your user story sounds finished. Template filled in, sounds good. But ask three people on your team what 'done' means, and you'll get three different answers.
This is acceptance criteria, written as Given, When, Then. It takes a vague feature request and turns it into one specific, testable condition anyone can check off.

display.code:
Given a team lead is on the reports page with 15+ team members shown
When they select a specific team member from the new filter
Then only that person's rows are shown, and a "Clear filter" control appears

beats.narration: The export button gets the same treatment: it has to respect the active filter, open cleanly in Excel and Sheets, and stamp the filename with the export date.

display.heading: Every story gets this treatment
display.subheading: Respects the active filter - Opens in Excel & Sheets - Filename includes the export date

beats.narration: Skip this step, and 'done' becomes a matter of opinion, and that gap is exactly where scope arguments happen late in a sprint.

display.heading: No acceptance criteria = no shared "done"
display.subheading: That gap is where scope disagreements happen late in a sprint
